summary: 是 shì links a subject to a noun: 我是学生 ‘I am a student’. It never changes (我是, 你是, 他们是 — present or past) and is negated with 不: 不是 bú shì. Two things English does with ‘to be’ are done differently: before an adjective Chinese uses no verb at all (我很好 ‘I am fine’ — never *我是好), and ‘to be somewhere’ is 在 zài: 老师在这里 ‘the teacher is here’.

blocks.caption: ‘To be’ in Chinese

blocks.title: No 是 before adjectives
blocks.text: 我很好, 她很高 — adjectives act like verbs. *我是好 is a typical beginner’s mistake (adjectives come in S16).

items.title: 是 — what something is
points: 我是老师。 I am a teacher.
这是门。 This is a door.

items.title: 在 — where something is
points: 老师在这里。 The teacher is here.
钥匙不在这里。 The keys are not here.

blocks.title: No articles after 是
blocks.text: ‘I am a student’ is 我是学生 — no word for ‘a’ is needed.

askYourself: Is the thing after ‘to be’ a noun (what someone or something is)? → 是.
Is it an adjective (how something is)? → no 是: 我很好.
Is it a place (where something is)? → 在: 他在这里.
Is the sentence negative? → 不是 / 不在 (bú shì, bú zài).
Does the verb change for person or time? → never.
steps: Choose 是 (noun), nothing (adjective) or 在 (place).
Negate with 不 directly before it.

traps: *我是好 / *我是很好 → 我很好.
*他没是老师 → 他不是老师 (是 is negated with 不 only).
*我是一个老师 is possible but usually just 我是老师 — no ‘a’ needed.

quiz.why: A noun after ‘to be’ needs 是.
是 is negated with 不, placed right before it.
不 becomes bú before the 4th tone.

seeAlso.note: Arabic has no ‘is’ in the present: ana ṭālib ‘I (am) a student’ — Chinese needs 是 between two nouns.
Hebrew too: ani talmid ‘I (am) a pupil’; and like Chinese, nothing stands before an adjective.
German sein conjugates (bin, bist, ist, sind) and is also used before adjectives (ich bin müde) — Chinese 我很累 has no verb.
